label: Measurements and Transformations
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 399 through 422 and answers two linked questions for Cayley-Klein geometry. How do we compute a distance or angle from the absolute conic, and which projective maps preserve those measurements. Both answers route through a single symmetric matrix, the bilinear form of the absolute.

label: The Measurement Problem
notes: Open by recalling that projective space has no built-in metric. A Cayley-Klein geometry adds one fixed object, the absolute conic, and reads every distance and angle as a cross-ratio against it. The chapter turns that cross-ratio recipe into an explicit closed formula in coordinates.

label: The Bilinear Form A
notes: Introduce the matrix A as the symmetric bilinear form whose zero set is the absolute conic. Stress the three scalars it produces from two points: the self-pairings P-transpose-A-P and Q-transpose-A-Q and the mixed pairing P-transpose-A-Q. These three numbers carry all metric information the chapter needs.

label: The Distance Formula
notes: State the central formula. The squared mixed pairing divided by the product of the two self-pairings is a projective invariant, and an inverse trigonometric or hyperbolic or logarithmic wrapper turns it into additive distance. Emphasize that the geometry type selects which wrapper appears.

label: Eliminating the Reference Points
notes: Explain that naively the distance needs the two points where the line meets the absolute. The chapter eliminates them. With the discriminant Delta built from the three Omega pairings, the cross-ratio of the endpoints is recovered directly, so X and Y never have to be constructed.

label: Orientation and the Reciprocal Class
notes: Warn students that the two absolute intersections have no canonical order. Swapping them sends the cross-ratio alpha to its reciprocal. So the honest projective datum is the unordered pair alpha and one over alpha, and the logarithm only fixes a sign once a direction is chosen.

label: Three Geometries, One Formula
notes: Lay out the comparison table. Elliptic geometry uses arccosine, hyperbolic geometry uses the logarithm or inverse hyperbolic cosine, and the Euclidean limit degenerates the primal form so the dual form carries the metric. One algebraic skeleton specializes to all three classical motion groups.

label: The Psi Comparison Formula
notes: Introduce the dual-conic expression Psi, built from the join of the two points paired through the dual matrix B and normalized by the self-pairings. Psi survives degeneration. For the Euclidean embedding it equals squared Euclidean distance, and a sign flip in B yields the pseudo-Euclidean square.

label: Isometries Preserve the Absolute
notes: Define a Cayley-Klein motion as a projective map whose matrix preserves the bilinear form, T-transpose-A-T proportional to A. Such a map sends the absolute conic to itself, hence permutes the line endpoints and preserves every cross-ratio, so all distances and angles are unchanged even when the affine grid distorts.

label: The Orthogonal Group of A
notes: Frame the isometry group as the projective orthogonal group of the form A. Choosing A as the identity gives the elliptic motions, a diagonal form with one negative sign gives the hyperbolic motions on the disk, and the degenerate Euclidean absolute recovers the familiar rigid motions of the plane.

label: Reflections Generate Motions
notes: Build motions from reflections. A center and its polar mirror form a pole-polar pair under A, giving an involution that preserves the absolute. Composing two reflections yields a rotation by twice the mirror angle when the mirrors meet inside the disk, and a hyperbolic translation when they meet outside.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by tying the threads together. Three Omega pairings feed one invariant ratio, one wrapper function names the geometry, and the orthogonal group of A is exactly the isometry group generated by reflections. Encourage students to revisit the notebook checks that verify conic preservation and the two-reflection rotation angle.
